turns.t: Mr. Dombrowski, come on in. I've got the letter from the clinic after your last COPD review here on the screen, and the nurse said you wanted to add something today.
Yeah. I coughed up some blood.
Okay, I'm glad you told us straight away. Tell me about it, as much as you can remember.
A streak. In the sink, after a coughing fit. Small, like a thread. Just the once.
A small streak of blood once. When was that, roughly? Days ago, weeks?
Not sure. Last week? Or the week before. I really can't say.
That's all right. Has it happened again since?
No. It's gone. Hasn't come back.
Good. And your usual cough, the one we've discussed before, is that any different from normal?
Same as always. Worse in the morning. I bring up some phlegm, then it eases off.
Is the phlegm clear, yellow, green? Any blood mixed in the rest of the time?
Clear mostly. No blood, just that one time.
Let me go through the medicines you're on now. Last time the list was a little hazy. Can you tell me what you take?
The tiotropium. 18 micrograms, once a day, in the morning. And the lisinopril, maybe 10 mg? I'd have to check the box.
Maybe 10 milligrams for the lisinopril, and we'll check the box. Anything else, like a rescue inhaler?
No. Only those two.
Fine, we'll tidy up the list afterwards. Quick tangent, since I'm curious. Does the tiotropium actually make a difference when you walk the dog?
Yes. I can go to the end of the block now. Before, I'd stop halfway.
That's a real improvement, good. Now, I noticed you've given up smoking. Remind me of the history?
Quit eight years ago. Smoked a pack a day for thirty years before that.
A pack a day for thirty years, and you stopped eight years ago. That took willpower. How's your chest and heart otherwise? Any chest pain or swelling in your legs?
No. Nothing like that. Heart's fine.
Good. And I have to ask, are you allergic to any medicines? It's on the record, but I want to double-check it.
Sulfa drugs. They give me hives. Big welts all over.
Sulfa drugs and hives, got it. I'll flag that on your file again. Let me listen to your chest now.
Take some slow, deep breaths in and out through your mouth.
I can hear a bit of wheeze on both sides, more at the bottom, which is in keeping with what you've had before. Now your neck, just to check.
What are you feeling for?
The glands. There are no enlarged lymph nodes, nothing lumpy. That's good news.
So what is it? The blood. Should I be worried?

I don't want to guess too much from one streak. In someone with your lung history, it could be irritation from all the coughing, but I can't rule out an infection, or something more serious in the lung yet.
Cancer?
I'm not saying that, and I'm not ignoring the question. It's one of the things we keep in mind with an ex-smoker, which is why we take a single streak seriously, even though it's gone.
Okay.
Here's the plan. I'd like to see you back in two weeks, and by then we'll know if it has come back or not. I'll go through everything with you properly then.
Two weeks. Fine.

Keep a note of anything you cough up, how much, and what colour. If you see more blood than a streak, or you get short of breath suddenly, come to the emergency department straight away, don't wait for the appointment.
More blood, or can't breathe. Got it.
Great. Keep taking your inhaler as you have been. And thanks for coming in right away, a lot of people sit on this for weeks.
My wife nagged me. See you in two weeks.
She's got the right idea. Take care, Mr. Dombrowski.

social_history.details: Smoked a pack a day for thirty years

physical_examination.finding: a bit of wheeze on both sides

clinical_assessment.assessment: rule out an infection, or something more serious in the lung
